baixa: Praça do Comércio, Rua Augusta and Rossio

The Baixa, the centre rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake: the great square on the Tagus with the Rua Augusta Arch, the pedestrian street up to Rossio square with its wave-patterned paving and, above, the Santa Justa Lift.
chiado: The elegant quarter on the hill, with its historic bookshops and Rua Garrett, the open-air ruins of the Carmo Convent and, a little higher, the São Pedro de Alcântara viewpoint overlooking the Baixa and the castle.
alfama: The oldest quarter, a maze of lanes with washing hung out, azulejos and houses stacked on the slope; the Sé (the cathedral), the Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol viewpoints over the Tagus and, if you're lucky, the yellow tram 28 brushing past the walls.
castelo: The Moorish fortress on the highest hill, with walls to walk along, towers and a panoramic terrace over the Baixa, the Tagus and the 25 de Abril bridge.
belem: The district on the Tagus from which the Portuguese explorers set sail: the Padrão dos Descobrimentos, the riverside walk, Belém Tower and, opposite, the façade of the Jerónimos Monastery. The must-stop is the pastéis de Belém, the custard tarts.
jeronimosins: The masterpiece of the Manueline style, paid for by the spice trade: the two-storey cloister with carved columns, the church with Vasco da Gama's tomb and the long façade facing the Tagus.
gulbenkian: One of Europe's finest collections: Egyptian and Islamic art, European painting with Rembrandt and Monet, Lalique's jewellery. The garden, open to all, is a quiet park in the city centre.
cais: Cais do Sodré, Bica and Rua Nova do Carvalho

The riverside quarter: the Mercado da Ribeira (Time Out Market, very touristy), the pink-painted Rua Nova do Carvalho, the Bica neighbourhood with the yellow Ascensor da Bica and the bars on the waterfront.
